# Nothing can say whether a cohort is admissible to a target

Refs neomjs/neo-agent-brain#77

## Context

Sub of neomjs/neo-agent-brain#77, from D#16304's criterion 4 resolution (@neo-opus-ada): the two audiences are **explicitly split**, and the recorded reason is the configuration-overlay surface — with the owner named as *the thing to fix*. This ticket is that thing.

## The Problem

**Nothing in the tree can answer "may this target take this cohort?"** — so selection has no predicate to consult, and the split the graduation recorded cannot be enforced.

Measured on `dev`:

- **Four daemons fail *closed* on config-overlay drift**, naming `--migrate-config` and exiting: `embed/daemon.mjs:51`, `message/daemon.mjs:32`, `wake/daemon.mjs:2884`, `orchestrator/daemon.mjs:63`. **Activation alone can produce a plane whose daemons refuse to boot.**
- **No admissibility surface exists.** `compatibilityContract`, `supportMatrix`, `minimumSupportedRevision`, `externallyAdmissible` return **zero hits** across `ai/`, `src/`, `buildScripts/`. Row **I** of the divergence matrix *proposes* one, which confirms none exists rather than merely suggesting it.

So "arbitrary `dev` cohorts are not externally admissible" is true and currently **unrepresentable** — the system cannot state it, let alone check it.

## The Architectural Reality

- `ai/scripts/lint/config-leaf-parity.json` already classifies `requiredDeploymentInputs`, `forbiddenEnv` and secrets. **The contract's raw material exists and is machine-readable**; what is missing is a predicate over it, expressed per cohort.
- `ai/scripts/setup/migrateConfigOverlay.mjs` migrates the `config.mjs` overlay and states explicitly it is *"never env-resolved values"* — so the env half is uncovered.
- **`#16447` is this ticket's superseded predecessor, not its written-prose complement.** *(Corrected 2026-08-04 — @neo-gpt and @neo-opus-ada both measured that this line still routed live authority to a closed ticket. It also misdescribed it.)* `#16447` began as *"make `MigrationPath.md` truthful"* and was **re-scoped by operator direction to be the executable delta itself** — the same shape as this ticket — then closed **NOT_PLANNED**. Its re-scope note is the reason this ticket is code and not prose: a hand-written guide *"serves an audience of zero and documents a manual runbook instead of removing it."* Nothing about a written guide is pending; this ticket carries the contract that neither of `#16447`'s two forms delivered.

## The Fix

Declare what makes a cohort admissible **for a given target**, derived from the existing census rather than hand-written: which required inputs it introduces, which keys it retires, and which overlay migrations it demands. Selection consults the predicate; a cohort that would land a plane in fail-closed boot is not admissible for that target.

## Contract Ledger Matrix

| Target Surface | Source of Authority | Proposed Behavior | Fallback / Error Semantics | Docs | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admissibility predicate | this ticket, over `config-leaf-parity.json` | Answers "may target T take cohort C?" with the reason when false | Unknown ⇒ **not admissible**; absence of evidence is never admissibility | contract docs | a cohort introducing a required input is inadmissible to a target lacking it |
| reason surface | this ticket | A false verdict names the blocking inputs/keys | Never a bare boolean — an unexplained refusal is unactionable | contract docs | the reason names the specific leaf |

## Decision Record impact

`none` — derives a predicate from an existing machine-readable census.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A predicate answers "may target T take cohort C?" and names the blocking required inputs / retired keys when the answer is no.
- [ ] It is **derived** from `config-leaf-parity.json` and each leaf's `requiredFor` metadata, not hand-maintained — a hand-list stales exactly as `MigrationPath.md` did. That staleness is the precedent, and it is what `#16447` originally existed to repair before it was re-scoped and closed.
- [ ] Unknown resolves to **not admissible**. Absence of evidence must never read as admissibility.
- [ ] The four fail-closed daemon guards are covered: a cohort introducing a required leaf is inadmissible to a target that lacks it.
- [ ] Selection (sibling sub) can consult the predicate; a refusal carries its reason into the ineligibility record.
- [ ] Nothing here widens or weakens the daemon guards — they stay fail-closed.

## Out of Scope

- **Changing the posture.** Whether we *should* commit to drop-in admissible cohorts and carry the migration burden is a decision, not a measurement, and the graduation deliberately left it open.
- **Relaxing any fail-closed guard.** The guards are correct; the missing piece is stating the contract they imply.
- **Writing the prose upgrade guide.** Out of scope because prose is the wrong carrier, **not** because another ticket owns it — `#16447` is closed **NOT_PLANNED** and owns nothing. The written path is produced *from* this predicate, for the deployment that needs it, once the capability exists.

## Avoided Traps

- **Treating absence of a compatibility contract as compatibility.** That is precisely today's failure mode: nothing says no, so everything looks admissible until a daemon exits at boot.
- **Hand-writing the contract.** `MigrationPath.md` is the standing precedent: a hand-maintained list of these same facts rots into a falsehood, which is why `#16447` was opened against it — and re-scoping that ticket away from prose, then closing it, is the team's recorded answer to repairing prose by hand a second time.

(`docker compose config` against its own ordered profile set, or the container's inspected

the shipped Compose file: if someone later templates that value, this test fails and the
contract note needs revisiting — which is the correct thing to be told rather than a brittle
assertion to be worked around.

missing was saying what it must be given.

At head 2976151d71, every one of these returned {admissible: true, evaluated: 0}:

  undefined · null · {} · a string · a number · [] · namespace nodes with no leaves

A loader that returned nothing, an import that failed, or a path aimed at the wrong tree all
arrive as an empty census — and an empty census read as "nothing blocked" is a PASS. The
weakest possible evidence produced the strongest possible verdict, on a predicate whose only
job is keeping a plane out of a fail-closed boot.

WHY I MISSED IT, since the shape is worth naming. I built the entire unknown-axis inversion
around "absence of evidence is never admissibility", mutation-proved it, and wrote it in the
module header. But that rule guards missing evidence about the TARGET. I never applied it to
missing evidence about the COHORT, and the header sentence read as though it covered both.
Proving absence-handling on one input and generalising to the other is not proof; my census
test even asserted `live.length > 0` against the real tree, which certifies the instrument
works rather than that the empty case is handled.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS LEAF DESCRIPTORS, NOT REQUIREMENTS, and that is the load-bearing choice
rather than the guard itself. A cohort carrying descriptors with zero `requiredFor` is fully
observed and legitimately demands nothing — it must stay ADMISSIBLE. A cohort with no
descriptors at all is not permissive, it is unread. Counting requirements collapses the two
and would manufacture a false inadmissible for every cohort that happens to constrain nothing
— the fix creating the failure direction I documented as the one this module cannot tolerate.
A real config tree carries hundreds of leaves whether or not any of them constrain anything,
so descriptors separate the states and requirements cannot.

Rendered as its own verdict, never as "NOT ADMISSIBLE — 0 blocking, 0 indeterminate". An
operator shown that would read a tool bug and re-run; the actionable fact is that the cohort
was never read and the fix is upstream of this predicate.

  discriminator counts requirements not descriptors     4 failed, 20 passed

The second is the one that matters: it proves the tests distinguish the two zero-states rather
than merely rejecting bad input.

The spec carries the positive control INSIDE the source-absence case — a real refusal with one
blocking row AND a real admissible on the same tree — so "refuses on bad input" cannot pass by

- 2026-08-04T14:44:16Z @tobiu referenced in commit `f0d8b07` - "feat(deploy): a predicate can answer whether a cohort is admissible to a target (#16453) (#16489)

* feat(deploy): a predicate can answer whether a cohort is admissible to a target (#16453)

Nothing in the tree could answer "may target T take cohort C?". Measured on dev:
compatibilityContract, supportMatrix, minimumSupportedRevision and externallyAdmissible
return zero hits across ai/, src/ and buildScripts/ — the question was unrepresentable,
not merely unanswered.

That matters because four daemons fail CLOSED when a required input is absent
(embed/daemon.mjs:51, message/daemon.mjs:32, wake/daemon.mjs:2884,
orchestrator/daemon.mjs:63) — each names --migrate-config and exits. So moving a lagging
deployment onto a newer cohort can produce a plane whose daemons refuse to boot, and the
only way to find out was to try it.

DERIVED, NEVER HAND-LISTED. The census is walked from the cohort's own config.data leaf
descriptors: 251 walked on the live tree, 5 carrying requiredFor. A hand-maintained list of
"inputs the new version needs" is exactly what staled in the written upgrade guide (#16447,
closed NOT_PLANNED), and it would stale the same way here — one leaf added without a
matching list edit and the predicate starts certifying a plane into a fail-closed boot.

UNKNOWN IS INADMISSIBLE, AND THAT DELIBERATELY INVERTS THE RUNTIME MATCHER. This is the
load-bearing decision and it is the opposite of what the runtime does.

ConfigProvider's matchesContext(list, actual) is `!list || list.includes(actual)`. With an
actual of `undefined` and a constraining list, that returns FALSE — the requirement does
not match, so the runtime treats the leaf as not-required and boots. Correct for a live
process, which knows its own entrypoint and mode by construction.

Reusing it here would have been catastrophic: a target whose mode we cannot state is a
target whose requirements we cannot evaluate, and answering "admissible" for it certifies
precisely the case we know least about. So an unstated axis that some requirement
constrains is reported INDETERMINATE and the verdict is not admissible. Absence of
evidence is never admissibility.

A refusal is never a bare boolean. It names the leaf, its env var and the requirement's own
reason, because an operator told "inadmissible" with nothing named cannot move their
deployment — which is how the written guide failed.

  orchestrator-daemon, NEO_AI_ORCHESTRATOR_AUTHORITY_PROFILE absent:

    NOT ADMISSIBLE — 1 blocking, 0 indeterminate.
      BLOCKING  orchestrator.authorityProfile (NEO_AI_ORCHESTRATOR_AUTHORITY_PROFILE)
                A role is declared, never inherited. Declare `container-plane` on the
                containerized Orchestrator (its Compose service sets it), or start the
                machine-local one with `npm run ai:host-edge`.

  Same target with the input declared: ADMISSIBLE.

For a lagging deployment that output IS the migration list, generated from the code.

MUTATION-PROVEN, per hop:

  unknown-axis adopts the runtime semantic (excluded)   2 failed, 11 passed
  presence-only (empty string counts as supplied)       1 failed, 12 passed

The second is not cosmetic: `NEO_X=` in a compose file reads as set to anything checking
presence and as empty to the readiness check that actually gates the boot, so a
presence-only predicate certifies a plane into the failure it exists to prevent. providesValue
mirrors ConfigProvider.isEmptyRequiredValue rather than reimplementing it loosely.

PLACEMENT: ai/scripts/setup/, beside migrateConfigOverlay.mjs — the sibling this ticket
names as covering the config-overlay half while stating it never handles env-resolved
values, which is the half left uncovered. isLeafDescriptor is mirrored rather than imported:
that module is a CLI with import-time side effects, and this one is consulted by selection.

Two probe errors caught by measuring rather than asserting, recorded because the first
looked like a product defect: testing entrypoint `orchestrator` returned ADMISSIBLE and I
nearly reported a false-admissible — the real entrypoint is `orchestrator-daemon`, so the
predicate was right and the probe was wrong.

Reads only. Migrates nothing, relaxes no guard, and the four fail-closed daemons are
untouched.

Refs #16453

* feat(deploy): the predicate names retired keys, and they are advisory rather than gating (#16453)

AC-1 names two halves — "the blocking required inputs / retired keys" — and the previous
commit built only the first. Re-reading the AC after committing is what caught it; the
predicate answered "what will refuse to boot" and was silent on "what you are still
carrying that no longer means anything".

collectLeafPaths walks every leaf a cohort declares, requirement-bearing or not.
diffCohortLeafSets({fromData, toData}) reports introduced and retired across a move, with
direction named rather than inferred from argument order.

ADVISORY, NEVER GATING — the load-bearing decision here.

A retired key cannot fail a readiness check. Nothing reads it, so no daemon exits on it,
so refusing the migration over one would block a move for zero safety gain — on exactly the
lagging deployments that most need to move. It is reported and the verdict stays admissible.

But it is reported on the ADMISSIBLE verdict too, which is the non-obvious half. A verdict
that says only "ADMISSIBLE" sends the operator into the migration still carrying the key,
and the failure mode is worse than an unused variable: the value LOOKS load-bearing in their
compose file, so the next person to read it preserves it as intentional. That is how an
inert setting outlives the code that gave it meaning.

Two boundaries, both tested because both are ways this becomes noise or a lie:

  a retired key the target does NOT set is not reported — it is a fact about the cohort,
  not a finding about the deployment, and reporting it trains operators to skim the section

  without a currentCohortData to compare against, retirement is NOT guessed — absence of a
  comparison point is not evidence that nothing retired. Same discipline as the unknown-axis
  rule in the previous commit: silence is not a clean bill.

Suite: 14 cases in the spec, 16 passed with chroma setup/teardown. 112 passed across
ai/scripts/setup/.

Refs #16453

* feat(deploy): the parity census supplies the REASON a key is forbidden, which no diff can derive (#16453)

Checking AC-2 honestly before writing a close claim turned up a real gap rather than a
wording quibble. The AC says the predicate is derived from `config-leaf-parity.json` AND
each leaf's `requiredFor` metadata. The two prior commits used the second source and none
of the first.

Reading the file changed what the gap was. `$composeDefaultParity.forbiddenEnv` is 22 keys
mapped to WRITTEN REASONS, and they are not one class:

  retired        NEO_AUTO_DREAM       "retired MCP-server startup control; the orchestrator owns Dream"
  derived        NEO_AUTH_*           "derived from auth.mode unless a narrower overlay opts out"
  posture-fixed  NEO_AI_DEPLOYMENT_MODE "cloud is the canonical config posture"

All three share one instruction — stop setting this — for three different reasons, and the
reason is the whole actionable payload. diffCohortLeafSets can derive THAT a key stopped
being declared. It cannot derive WHY, because the fact is not in either tree. "No longer
declared" names the symptom; "the orchestrator owns Dream" tells an operator what replaced it.

So the parity map is now consulted for two things: a reason for each diff-derived retirement
when it has one, and an independent forbidden-keys pass.

INDEPENDENT IS THE POINT. The forbidden pass needs no currentCohortData. A plane far enough
behind that nobody recorded what it was built from has no comparison cohort, so the diff is
structurally unavailable — and that is exactly the deployment most likely to be carrying dead
keys. The surface that needs it most is the one the diff cannot serve.

ADVISORY, and that is evidential rather than cautious. lint-config-template-ssot.mjs enforces
this map against OUR Compose profiles in OUR CI. Nothing measured shows a foreign plane
refusing to boot on a forbidden key, so gating would assert a failure mode I have not
observed — the same error in the opposite direction from the unknown-axis rule.

Deduped: a key can be both diff-retired and parity-forbidden. Two rows for one key reads as
two problems and costs a reconciliation that yields nothing, so the merged row keeps the
parity reason over the generic diff wording.

MUTATION-PROVEN, per decision:

  presence-only instead of providesValue   1 failed, 19 passed
  dedupe filter removed                    1 failed, 19 passed

The live-map case asserts against the shipped file rather than a restated string, so the
test cannot keep passing against a copy that has drifted from it.

that satisfies it. A probe written after the feature only proves the feature agrees
with itself; the red-first order is what tests the probe.

It gets its OWN opt-in project rather than a spec inside `integration-parity`.
Reusing that project was the cheaper edit and the wrong one: it is already in the
default CI gate, and this scenario is red by design while the implementation leaves
are open, so it would have turned the shared gate red on day one — the trap the
source ticket names against itself. Verified: `update-chain` appears in no
`.github/workflows/` file, while `integration-parity` does, which is the positive
control that the check can detect gate membership at all.

Opt-in rather than skipped, deliberately. A `test.skip` inside a gated project reads
as green and proves nothing; an unreferenced config cannot read as anything.

Two properties carry the value:

The red names WHICH leg is missing, with owner and obligation, so the failure is a
work list rather than an opaque wall — five legs today (#16450, #16451, #16452,
#16453, #16320), with the one shipped leg asserted by name so a sibling landing
cannot go unnoticed.

An unrunnable scenario reports INCONCLUSIVE and FAILS. A harness that cannot
provision has measured nothing, and reporting that as green would make the goal bar
satisfiable by breaking the harness.

Also: `retries: 0`. A flaky goal bar is not a goal bar — a scenario that passes on
attempt two has told you the chain is unreliable, and retrying converts that
finding into a green tick.

It implements NONE of the machinery it measures: no caller, no selector, no
admissibility rule. Growing those would make it a second umbrella wearing a sub's
label, which is the failure that produced this leaf.

Observed: 1 passed (the runnability contract), 1 failed with all five missing legs
named. That is the intended state."
